title: Sorghum flour, white, pearled, unenriched, dry, raw

content.title: About
content.content: Sorghum flour is a finely milled grain product made from cleaned and pearled sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) kernels. The white pearled flour has a light color, fine texture, and neutral flavor, making it versatile for baking and cooking. The product is not enriched with additional vitamins or minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sorghum is one of the most drought‑tolerant crops, grown in arid regions of Africa, Asia, and the United States.
Pearling removes the outer bran layer, resulting in a lighter, softer flour.
Sorghum flour is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for gluten‑free diets.
Compared with corn flour, sorghum flour has a higher protein content (about 10‑12 %).
Sorghum has been used in traditional cuisines long before wheat became widespread.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Sorghum flour provides more protein than most other gluten‑free alternatives, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Sorghum flour raises blood sugar more slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in sorghum help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sorghum allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to sorghum products.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or fermenting the flour can mitigate this.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Manufacturing facilities may have gluten cross‑contamination, which is important for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sorghum flour can be used in breads, pancakes, cookies, muffins, and as a thickener for sauces. It blends well with other gluten‑free flours. For better leavening, add baking powder or use a sourdough starter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
